chapter: New York Pops and later work
title: Union membership and residuals
summary: Joining the New York and Hollywood unions, tiny residuals and film clip rights costs.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Did you have to do that, isn’t there a six month period when you come to New York for the union, to get in the union?
No, I had to do it in Hollywood though.

No New York, see I came to New York, NBC signed — when I came to New York I started doing, with strength, the Lucky Strike Show in New York as a conductor so they couldn’t say anything about that. And I guess, I don’t know how the devil I got into it, I guess the New York Local just gave up and probably made me a member you know, because I still belonged to 47 and 10 and the Guild in England. But in Hollywood, when I went to Hollywood, it was almost a year. Six months was the law, but it was almost a year before I got anything, and I mean I played rehearsal piano for everybody, but oh, never in studio orchestras.
Do you get residuals from your work over the years in Hollywood?
Very little. Very, very little. It’s better the last, what, fifteen years I suppose. But the golden years, gone.

Yeah, there’s nothing. Well it’s our own fault too. Or I don’t know whether it’s anybody’s fault. Sometimes it bothers me, especially when you’re looking for something, like when I did my 80th birthday gala, there were snippets of film that I wanted to use that were meaningful to me, but some guy in Pretoria, Ohio owns, you know, he’s bought the rights, and he wants ten thousand dollars, I mean for a minute and a half of film. Maybe we’re all wrong. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
